title: Anaphora With Non-nominal Antecedents in Computational Linguistics: a Survey
research_question: What linguistic properties, annotation practices, computational approaches, resources, and unresolved problems characterize anaphora whose antecedents are non-nominal and denote abstract entities such as events, facts, situations, or propositions?
methodology: The paper conducts a structured survey and synthesis of theoretical, corpus-annotation, rule-based, statistical, and neural work on non-nominal-antecedent anaphora. It compares competing terminologies, analyzes the syntax and semantics of anaphors and their antecedents, reviews prominent annotated corpora, and summarizes automatic resolution systems and their reported evaluations. The survey concentrates primarily on English and uses tables to compare corpora, annotation choices, system architectures, and performance metrics.

key_findings.finding: Non-nominal anaphora is computationally difficult because potential antecedents have diverse syntactic forms, the candidate space is large, antecedent boundaries can be unclear, and ordinary nominal-coreference features such as gender and number are generally unavailable.

The referent evoked from the same linguistic antecedent can be interpreted at different semantic types, such as an event, proposition, or fact, and the predication context of the anaphor provides important constraints on that interpretation.
Precisely delimiting non-nominal antecedent spans is a central annotation problem and is associated with low or only moderate inter-annotator agreement in several annotation efforts.
Only a limited number of annotated corpora reviewed by the survey are reusable, and many available corpora are small for supervised machine-learning purposes.
Older rule-based resolution approaches often remain competitive with statistical approaches, motivating combinations of explicit linguistic knowledge with modern data-driven representations.

Whether a resolver must identify an exact antecedent text span is application-dependent; some applications may primarily need the abstract semantic type, whereas others need explicit textual grounding.

Current formulations inadequately handle antecedents that are discontinuous or extend across more than one sentence, so proposition-level reference cannot always be reduced to selection of one contiguous local span.

limitations: The survey explicitly focuses mostly on English, so its synthesis does not fully characterize language-specific phenomena in other languages.
The authors state that the survey only scratches the surface of the semantics and pragmatics of reference to event-like and other abstract entities.
The surveyed studies use heterogeneous corpora, annotation schemes, target expressions, and evaluation measures, which limits direct comparison of reported system performance.
Much of the available empirical literature reviewed by the paper relies on relatively small annotated datasets.
The review necessarily reflects work available up to 2018 and therefore does not cover subsequent developments.
raw_claims: Non-nominal antecedents commonly evoke abstract entities such as events, facts, propositions, and situations.
A non-nominal antecedent need not correspond to an easily delimited noun phrase or other conventional discourse referent.
The semantic interpretation of an anaphor can differ from the basic semantic type contributed by its antecedent.
Predicates surrounding an anaphor can constrain whether its referent is interpreted as an event, proposition, fact, or another abstract type.
Demonstratives such as this and that are important forms for reference to non-nominal antecedents.
Shell nouns can package proposition-like content and participate in anaphoric relations with non-nominal material.
Identifying exact antecedent boundaries is one of the main sources of annotation disagreement.
Few reviewed corpora are both reusable and large enough to support modern supervised learning comfortably.
Rule-based systems encode linguistic constraints that remain potentially useful to data-driven models.
The usefulness of recovering an exact antecedent string depends on the downstream application.
Some abstract antecedents are discontinuous or span multiple sentences, which complicates span-based resolution.
